title: IEEE PELS University Lab Kit
tools: CAD, PLA 3D printing, client coordination, manufacturing and shipping
evidence: Printed bases · 200+ printed-part sets manufactured and shipped

description: Adapted lab-kit bases for printing without supports and managed manufacturing and shipping of more than 200 complete printed-part sets.
takeaway: I adapted the lab kit’s printed bases and managed manufacturing and shipping of more than 200 complete printed-part sets.
overviewHeading: From a mounting detail to a production run.
overview: The IEEE Power Electronics Society’s University Lab Kit gives students a platform for hands-on power-electronics experiments. At Illinois MakerLab, I adapted the supplied base designs for 3D printing and worked with the client on the mounting arrangement.

I designed fitted slots for square nuts so circuit boards could be secured with 4-40 × ¾-inch screws, removed for debugging, and reinstalled. I used PLA and adapted the bases to print without supports, refining the mounting arrangement through qualitative fit checks and design iterations.
I then scaled production through MakerLab and managed manufacturing and shipping of more than 200 complete sets of printed parts. The electronics and other kit components were handled separately.

story.heading: Making the boards removable
paragraphs: The University Lab Kit is an educational power-electronics platform. My scope at Illinois MakerLab was the printed mechanical base and its production, starting from the kit team’s supplied design. The mounting arrangement needed to secure the boards while allowing them to be removed and reinstalled for debugging.

I worked with the client on that arrangement and designed fitted slots for square nuts in the printed mounting posts. The boards fasten with 4-40 × ¾-inch screws. This keeps the connection removable and avoids adhesive or a separate heat-set-insert installation operation.

story.heading: Designing around the production process
paragraphs: I used PLA for the printed bases and adapted the model for printing without supports. At production scale, this avoids repeating a support-removal operation on every set of components.

I assessed fit qualitatively and revised the design iteratively. This was a practical check of the printed mounting arrangement; I did not establish a numerical tolerance or joint-strength rating. The photographs show the current bases with the nuts seated in their slots.

story.heading: Following the printed parts through delivery
paragraphs: I organized and managed manufacturing and shipping of more than 200 complete sets of printed parts through MakerLab. My responsibilities connected the mechanical changes, client communication, production, and delivery of those parts.

The quantity refers to complete sets of printed components. Electronics and the other kit components were handled separately. The project website acknowledges my contribution and Illinois MakerLab’s support, while the original kit design remains credited to its development team.

story.heading: What I took from the production run
paragraphs: A small mounting detail had consequences for both use and production. The nut slots made board removal possible, while the support-free geometry avoided an extra cleanup step across the run.

The result was more than 200 complete printed-part sets manufactured and shipped. A fuller production record would add slot dimensions, nut specifications, print settings, and measured acceptance criteria; the qualitative checks do not establish production yield or long-term joint performance.

attribution: Original kit design: IEEE PELS University Lab Kit team. The project website acknowledges my contribution and Illinois MakerLab’s support.

summary: I adapted the printed bases of an educational power-electronics kit so circuit boards could be screwed in and removed for debugging. Fitted square-nut slots and printing without supports reduced assembly operations. I then managed manufacturing and shipping of 200+ complete printed-part sets through Illinois MakerLab.

title: Tape Spring Hinge
tools: Abaqus, MATLAB, camera measurements, vibration and bending tests

takeaway: I tested a flexible steel hinge in several ways to find which parts of its behavior the model could predict.

description: Built and tested a flexible steel hinge, comparing its shape, vibration, and bending response with Abaqus models.
overview: A tape spring can fold and recover using the flexibility of a thin curved strip. I prepared a steel specimen and compared its shape, vibration, and bending response with models in Abaqus and MATLAB.
The second vibration frequency matched within about 5%, while other modes differed more. The nonlinear bending simulation also stopped before completing the measured response.

Checking several behaviors made the comparison more useful: a close result in one test could not establish that the model captured the hinge’s full motion. The project gave me measured evidence for where the assumptions needed further attention.

story.heading: One hinge, several different checks
paragraphs: A tape spring forms a localized fold by changing the curvature of a thin strip. Its geometry, vibration, and bending response answer different design questions: where the hinge forms, how the mounted structure moves, and what moment is needed to bend it.

I prepared the steel specimen, fixtures, and optical measurements, developed the analytical and Abaqus comparisons, and processed the test data in MATLAB. I treated the static shape measurements, screwdriver-tap vibration test, pull-and-release sequence, and three-point bending tests as separate evidence.

story.heading: Checking the shape against the thin-strip model
paragraphs: The analytical model treats the strip as a thin, isotropic, elastic plate. Minimizing its bending energy predicts a localized hinge radius equal in magnitude to the original transverse radius. The nominal reference in the report was 16.25 mm.

I applied a speckle pattern, calibrated the stereo-camera setup, and captured the deployed, equal-sense, and opposite-sense configurations in printed fixtures. In MATLAB I filtered invalid surface points, estimated a cylinder axis using principal components, and fitted a cylinder to each measured surface.

The two bent configurations were close to the nominal radius, but the deployed surface was not. A single fitted cylinder is an approximation to a surface that may contain flattening or twist, so a small fitting residual does not remove uncertainty from the specimen or fixture.

equation.spoken: Plate bending stiffness D equals E times thickness cubed divided by twelve times one minus Poisson ratio squared.
equation.explanation: The ideal plate stiffness depends on the cube of thickness. Geometry and material assumptions therefore matter when comparing a very thin strip with a physical fixture.

table.caption: Cylinder-fit radii for the same tape-spring specimen

story.heading: Separating vibration measurement from deployment
paragraphs: For vibration, I tapped the mounted strip with a screwdriver and recorded its displacement at 2,000 frames per second. I removed the mean displacement before applying an FFT to the exported data. The DIC software and MATLAB analyses used the same recording; they were two processing routes, not independent physical tests.

The second measured peak was closest to the Abaqus prediction. The first and third peaks differed more, so the result supports a limited comparison of the mounted system rather than validation of every mode. Idealized material properties, the clamp, printed fixtures, and surface markings are possible contributors to the mismatch; their individual effects were not isolated.

table.caption: Measured peaks and modeled natural frequencies

story.heading: What the release sequence can show
paragraphs: I also bent and released the strip while recording it from the side. This view made the recovery, overshoot, twisting, and decay visible, but the speckle pattern was not clear enough for a full quantitative DIC reconstruction.
I used selected frames to describe the motion qualitatively. They are not the source of the FFT frequencies, a measured deployment-time specification, or a calibrated damping coefficient.

story.heading: Comparing bending moment, not just machine force
paragraphs: The three-point bending tests used a 120 mm support span, 25 mm travel, and a loading rate of 10 mm/min. I tested both bending directions and converted the machine’s force and crosshead displacement into moment and an effective bending angle for comparison with theory.

The Abaqus bending model used a shortened 120 mm strip with prescribed end constraints rather than explicitly modeling the loading nose and supports. That reduced contact complexity, but it also changed how closely the model represented the physical fixture.

The measured opposite-sense response had a sharp peak followed by a lower plateau. The plateau is the more appropriate comparison with a steady-state bending-moment prediction. The static nonlinear simulation stopped near its positive peak when it failed to converge, so it did not reproduce the full measured response.

sources.label: Bending setup and model, PDF pp. 23–26

story.heading: What I would carry into a follow-up study
paragraphs: The useful result is a map of where the assumptions held and where they did not. The bent radii followed the simple geometric prediction more closely than the deployed radius; modal agreement varied; and the nonlinear bending comparison remained incomplete.

Further work needs better characterization of the mounted boundary conditions and a numerical treatment that can continue through the instability. Repeating the tests and measuring local rotation directly would help separate the strip’s response from fixture and crosshead effects. Those are next steps, not completed improvements.

summary: Can a thin curved steel strip act as a predictable hinge? I prepared and tested the specimen, using optical shape measurements, a tap test, and bending experiments to check the model. Its second vibration frequency matched within about 5%, while other modes and nonlinear bending exposed limits in the assumptions.

description: Designed and assembled printed folding mechanisms, adjusting panel thickness and clearance so solid parts could move together.
overview: A pattern that folds in paper can jam when its panels have thickness. I designed rigid-panel mechanisms in NX, changing panel thicknesses and adding cutouts to give the moving parts room.
I prepared the designs, assembled the printed panels with tape hinges, and checked their motion by hand. Nikhil submitted the print job on the Space Structures Lab-managed printer.

The Bennett-linkage prototype demonstrated coordinated folding, and a related Miura-Ori assembly explored another pattern. These were working demonstrations of the geometry; strength and repeated-use durability were not tested.

story.heading: Turning a paper mechanism into solid panels
paragraphs: The starting point was an assigned four-panel, single-vertex folding pattern. In paper, the fold lines can meet at a vertex with negligible thickness. Giving those panels thickness creates interference unless the hinge axes and panel geometry are changed.

I folded a paper model to examine the coordinated motion, then used Bennett-linkage conditions to define the hinge offsets for rigid panels. My work covered the geometric calculations, NX models, fabrication preparation, assembly, and manual evaluation.

story.heading: Using hinge offsets to make room for thickness
paragraphs: The assigned sector angles were 30°, 90°, 150°, and 90°. Opposing pairs sum to 180°, satisfying the stated flat-foldability conditions. With the prescribed 5 mm first offset, the Bennett ratio gives a 10 mm adjacent offset and the repeating offset set 5, 10, 5, 10 mm.

I modeled the wedge-shaped panels and checked the perpendicular distances between adjacent hinge axes in the assembled CAD model. The panels did not all have the same thickness; two had thickness changes within the panel. This accommodated the offset geometry and reduced the interference that a uniform-thickness translation of the paper pattern would create.

equation.spoken: The ratio of hinge offsets a twelve to a twenty three equals sine thirty degrees divided by sine ninety degrees, or one half.
equation.explanation: With a₁₂ = 5 mm, the adjacent hinge offset a₂₃ is 10 mm. The offset distances constrain the CAD geometry rather than being arbitrary clearances.

sources.label: Thickness and clearance choices, PDF p. 7

story.heading: Assembling and checking the Bennett mechanism
paragraphs: After preparing the models for printing, I assembled the rigid parts using masking-tape hinges along the intended hinge axes. Hinge placement was part of the mechanism: moving an axis would change the geometric compatibility even if the panels themselves matched the CAD.

The physical assembly showed coordinated motion when actuated by hand. The result is qualitative evidence that the panel geometry and hinge arrangement could fold together. It does not measure actuation force, structural stiffness, hinge accuracy, or cycle life.
Nikhil submitted the print job on the Space Structures Lab-managed printer. I performed the design, preparation, assembly, and evaluation described here.

story.heading: Extending the work to a Miura-Ori pattern
paragraphs: I also created a thick-panel Miura-Ori base unit in NX and assembled three printed units into a larger folding pattern. This was a related extension, rather than a second demonstration of the full Bennett derivation.

The repeated assembly let me examine whether neighboring units could be aligned and connected using the same taped-hinge approach. The photos show the combined structure in several manually folded configurations.

story.heading: What the prototypes establish
paragraphs: The Bennett specimen connects a geometric compatibility condition to a real, foldable assembly. The Miura-Ori example shows a larger patterned build using repeated thick-panel units.

The next engineering step would be to define repeatable hinge hardware and quantify motion, interference margins, and loads. The taped prototypes were useful for checking kinematics; they were not qualified as load-carrying deployable structures.

summary: Paper folds easily until the panels have thickness. I used Bennett-linkage geometry to place hinge axes 5 and 10 mm apart, then designed and assembled printed panels with clearance for motion. A hand-folded Bennett mechanism and a three-unit Miura-Ori extension demonstrated the geometry in physical parts.

title: Thin Origami Bellows
tools: NX crease-pattern design, paper fabrication, tensile testing, data analysis

description: Designed and folded a paper bellows, then tested how it opened under tension and examined tearing near its attachment.
overview: I designed a paper bellows to study how a folded structure opens under tension. I created the crease pattern in NX, made the specimen, and tested it using printed fixtures.
The single trial reached 48.1 N before tearing near an attachment. That result describes this specimen and test setup, rather than a repeatable strength rating.

The test made the load transfer into the paper a clear issue for further work. Better attachments and repeat tests would be needed to separate the bellows’ opening behavior from the limits of the setup.

story.heading: Building the prescribed folding geometry
paragraphs: The task was to manufacture a thin-sheet bellows and examine its resistance to opening under axial tension. I modeled the assigned pattern in NX: four repeating units, 12 mm facet width, and 45° crease angles, including tabs to close the sheet into a tube.

I printed the pattern on 11 × 17-inch paper, cut the boundary, scored the fold lines, and formed the bellows. Double-sided tape closed the longitudinal seam. I checked that the assembled specimen could compress and extend without obvious interference before mounting it for testing.

I carried out the CAD, fabrication, test, and analysis, with fixture guidance from the Space Structures Lab. The paper grade and thickness were not formally recorded, which limits reproduction of the specimen.

story.heading: Making the fixture part of the experiment
paragraphs: The bellows was taped to printed end attachments and mounted vertically in an Instron frame. The lower end remained fixed while the crosshead pulled the upper end upward. The intended boundary was approximately clamped, but tape and attachment compliance could contribute to the measured motion.

The loading rate was approximately 0.20 mm/s, with force and displacement sampled at about 20 Hz. Only one specimen and one trial were available. No external extensometer measured the bellows locally, so the displacement record includes any grip seating and fixture motion as well as opening of the paper structure.

sources.label: Fixtures and test method, PDF pp. 6–8

story.heading: Reading the peak together with the recorded range
paragraphs: The saved record began at approximately 32.5 N, already under tension, and covered 4.449 mm of crosshead travel. I converted the machine position to travel relative to the first recorded point, then normalized it to the final recorded travel.

That normalized percentage describes the saved data window. It is not proof that the bellows completed its full geometric deployment. The result plot emphasizes the early part of this normalized record, where the force rises to 48.1 N and then drops sharply as tearing develops near an attachment.
The peak therefore belongs to this specimen and its attachment conditions. A single, preloaded trial cannot establish repeatable deployment force or the intrinsic strength of the crease pattern.

equation.spoken: Recorded deployment percentage equals crosshead position minus the initial recorded position, divided by the total recorded travel, times one hundred.
equation.explanation: Zero and 100% are the ends of the recorded crosshead-travel range. They are not independently measured fully compressed and fully deployed geometric states.

story.heading: What the failure makes worth testing next
paragraphs: The abrupt force loss and tearing near the attachment make load introduction a central part of the result. The experiment does not isolate crease resistance from damage at the fixture-paper interface.

A follow-up needs a documented paper specification, improved attachments, a zero-load record, direct displacement measurement, and repeated specimens. Those changes would help distinguish the folding response from setup compliance and local tearing. They were not completed within this project.

summary: I designed, folded, and tested a paper bellows to investigate how its crease pattern resists opening. The single tensile trial peaked at 48.1 N before tearing near an attachment. The result made fixture compliance and load transfer central to interpreting the response, rather than treating the peak as a material-strength rating.

description: Led fabrication of a carbon-fiber beam, revising the core preparation and cure setup before the team’s load test.
overview: Our team designed a carbon-fiber I-beam for a 7,200 lbf load target. I led fabrication, turning the numerical design into a physical beam using the materials, tooling, and cure equipment available to us.

We changed the core preparation when foam filling proved impractical, then revised the cure setup after the flanges warped. The team’s tested Nomex-core beam reached 2,376 lbf—about one-third of the target.

The test exposed a substantial gap between the design prediction and the manufactured beam. My part of the project was working through the build decisions and documenting the process behind that result.

story.heading: A load target constrained by the build
paragraphs: The team’s objective was a carbon-fiber/epoxy I-beam for a 7,200 lbf three-point-bending load target. I led fabrication from the numerical design, working within the available prepreg, steel-channel tooling, bagging materials, and autoclave equipment.

The team assigned longitudinal 0° reinforcement to the flange faces and ±45° reinforcement to the web facings, reflecting the bending and shear load paths. Nomex honeycomb separated and supported the web facings. Available tooling restricted the web height, so the build could not simply use the largest section allowed by the competition envelope.
The numerical design and aggregate test results were team work. The fabrication decisions, layup, assembly, and process revisions are the part of the project I led.

sources.label: Load paths and design constraints, PDF pp. 13–20

story.heading: Replacing a core preparation that would not bond flat
paragraphs: The initial concept stacked two Nomex honeycomb sheets and filled them with expanding polyurethane foam. The foam stiffened the core, but expansion forced the sheets apart and left a rough, curved surface. Sanding did not produce the flat interface needed to bond the laminate facings.

We removed the foam and used Hysol EA 9696 .06 adhesive film between the Nomex layers and between the core and facings. This addressed the bonding-surface problem without treating foam filling as a completed manufacturing solution.

I worked through the layup and assembly around the tooling and available prepreg. The web used segmented angle-ply material because the available prepreg width did not cover the full beam length; the report’s alternating cutting arrangement attempted to support adjacent layers at these interfaces.

sources.label: Core trials and web cutting arrangement, PDF pp. 30–34

story.heading: Learning that bag pressure was not enough restraint
paragraphs: The first beam was cured on its side, leaving both flanges unsupported by the autoclave platform. The report records 125°C for 1 hour 45 minutes with 5 psi autoclave pressure. As the resin softened, the unconstrained flanges relaxed outward and the bag tended to flatten the section.

For the second build, we cured the beam upright. The platform restrained the lower flange, an aluminum plate restrained the upper flange, and C-clamps joined the mold channels. The revised process used 115°C and approximately 0 psi reported autoclave pressure, while the vacuum bag and mechanical tooling held the assembly.

The revision produced a testable beam, but it did not eliminate every imperfection. Rippling remained near the vacuum-port side, where the connector and plate arrangement interfered with consolidation. The manufactured specimen weighed 432.4 g.

sources.label: Cure conditions and process changes, PDF pp. 31–35

story.heading: Testing the manufactured structure
paragraphs: The team tested the beam in a three-point-bending setup at the Newmark Structural Engineering Laboratory, with a 23-inch support span and an approximately 1 in/min crosshead rate. The source analysis removed an initial seating region before deriving flexural properties.

The report distinguishes initial failure from subsequent loading and progressive damage. Its load-displacement plot includes multiple peaks, so later load-carrying capacity should not be read as an undamaged elastic response.

sources.label: Test method and response, PDF pp. 37–43

story.heading: Comparing the result with what the model actually predicted
paragraphs: The beam reached 2,376 lbf against the 7,200 lbf target. The team’s idealized analysis predicted first-ply failure near 7,700 lbf and a flexural modulus of 45.95 GPa; the modulus derived from test data was 14.63 GPa.

The prediction used laminate and beam-theory assumptions, including idealized load transfer and material properties that were not all measured for the specimen. The report also identified a core-shear risk, so the laminate first-ply estimate was not a complete prediction of every possible failure mode.

Damage was observed in the web rather than following the predicted upper-flange sequence. The report discusses discontinuities between angle-ply segments, bonding and consolidation, and out-of-plane effects as possible contributors. The data do not isolate a single cause or quantify each contribution.

table.caption: Team design predictions and the documented Nomex-core test
rows: Flange rippling and process imperfections remained

sources.label: Derived properties and failure discussion, PDF pp. 41–44

story.heading: What this build changed in my approach
paragraphs: The core and cure trials made manufacturing constraints visible before the destructive test. A usable bonding surface and positive flange restraint were necessary just to carry the design into testable hardware. The final load result then showed that a testable part still could fall far short of the structural target.

For further development, the report points toward better vacuum-port placement, more uniform consolidation, and a review of core, joint, and ply-interface assumptions. Those improvements remain to be tested. The results here cover the documented Nomex-core beam.

featuredCaption: Led fabrication of a carbon-fiber I-beam, revising the core preparation and cure setup before the team’s load test.
summary: I led fabrication of a carbon-fiber I-beam from the team’s numerical design. Expanding foam disrupted the core’s bonding surface, and the first cure warped the flanges. We revised both processes to produce a testable beam; its 2,376 lbf result exposed the gap to the 7,200 lbf target.

title: Bistable Composite Boom

description: Modeled, built, and measured a carbon-fiber boom that holds both a coiled and an extended shape.
overview: A deployable boom needs to pack away compactly and hold a useful shape when extended. I modeled, fabricated, and measured a thin carbon-fiber specimen that could stay in either configuration without being held.
The measurements of how tightly each shape curved were within about 5% of the model’s predictions for this specimen. I then screened 5,476 simulated layer arrangements to explore alternatives.

That comparison showed a useful tradeoff: lowering the estimated energy needed to switch shapes also changed the coiled geometry. A design needed to meet both requirements. The alternative arrangements remained simulations.

story.heading: A boom with two useful equilibrium shapes
paragraphs: A deployable boom needs a compact stored configuration and a useful extended configuration. The lab specimen used a symmetric, three-ply [45° plain weave / 0° unidirectional / 45° plain weave] carbon-fiber laminate to hold both shapes without an external fixture maintaining them.

I carried the work from MATLAB laminate and energy modeling into layup, vacuum bagging, curing, stereo-camera measurement, and geometry processing. I then used the model to screen alternative layups rather than assuming the fabricated baseline was the only option.

story.heading: Reducing the shape model to curvature and axis angle
paragraphs: I assembled the laminate extensional, bending-extension, and bending stiffness matrices from the transformed ply properties. The thin-shell model assumed perfect bonding, small strains, linear orthotropic elasticity, and no residual manufacturing strain.

Under the stated cylindrical slit-boom assumptions, each configuration is represented by a cylinder curvature C and an axis angle θ relative to the boom length. I evaluated a strain-energy landscape and searched for distinct local minima, treating angles 0° and 180° as the same physical orientation.
This reduction makes the model practical to search, but it does not reproduce every local wrinkle, residual stress, or edge effect in a manufactured laminate.

equation.spoken: Cylinder curvature C is the reciprocal of radius R.
equation.explanation: The same curvature definition is used for the model and the cylinder fitted to the camera measurements, so their geometric results can be compared directly.

sources.label: Laminate and energy model, PDF pp. 5–7

story.heading: Fabricating and measuring the baseline
paragraphs: I laid up the plain-weave/unidirectional/plain-weave stack on the provided cylindrical mold, whose nominal diameter was 60.325 mm. The stated ply thicknesses were 58.2 μm for plain weave and 40.0 μm for unidirectional prepreg. I vacuum-bagged the laminate and oven-cured it under vacuum.

For measurement, I applied a white speckle pattern, adjusted the camera focus and lighting, and calibrated the stereo DIC setup with a reference plate. Five captures of each configuration were averaged pointwise. These were repeated captures of one specimen, not five separate builds.

In MATLAB, I removed invalid coordinates, fitted a cylinder to each surface, and used an unwrapped point cloud and singular-value decomposition to recover the axis angle. The cylinder-fit residual describes agreement with that fitted surface; it is not a complete measurement-uncertainty bound.

sources.label: Fabrication and DIC processing, PDF pp. 8–11

story.heading: Comparing both stable states before tuning the model
paragraphs: The measured curvatures differed from the baseline predictions by about 4.8% in the deployed state and 4.6% in the coiled state, using the analytical prediction as the denominator. The measured coiled angle was also a few degrees away from the nominal 90°.

I separately explored bounded changes in forming radius, ply angles, and effective ply thickness to see whether plausible manufacturing variation could reduce the discrepancy. The search improved agreement with the same measurements. That is calibration, not independent validation or a direct measurement of the actual ply thickness.

table.caption: Baseline predictions and DIC-derived geometry for one specimen

story.heading: Asking what easier switching would cost
paragraphs: The coarse design screen covered 5,476 combinations across four symmetric, three-ply families using the available plain-weave and unidirectional prepregs. Outer- and middle-ply angles varied in 5° increments. The forming radius and nominal material inputs stayed fixed for the screen.

I ranked candidates using an estimated strain-energy barrier between stable configurations. The lowest reported candidate was UD/UD/UD with −25° outer plies and a 30° middle ply. Its coiled-like state became less curved and moved away from the original 90° orientation.

The optimization therefore exposed competing objectives: a smaller estimated barrier did not guarantee a compact coil. A final selection would need explicit constraints on both stable shapes rather than ranking energy alone.

sources.label: Layup screen and tradeoff, PDF pp. 15–17

story.heading: Where the evidence stops
paragraphs: The physical result is the fabricated baseline and its two measured stable configurations. The alternative layups remained numerical candidates, and the modeled transition barrier was not measured as an actuation force or demonstrated as the true minimum-energy transition path.

A useful next stage would fabricate a candidate that also satisfies storage geometry, then measure its stable shapes and switching response independently. The present study provides the comparison method and a reason to make the design objective more complete.

summary: I modeled and fabricated a composite boom that holds both an extended and a coiled shape. Optical measurements put its two curvatures within about 5% of the baseline predictions. I then screened 5,476 layups and found that reducing the estimated switching-energy barrier could compromise the shape needed for compact storage.

description: Mapped how a proposed medical-drone control center would handle delivery requests, plan missions, and exchange information with aircraft and ground teams.
overview: A medical-drone delivery involves more than the aircraft. A request has to become a mission, the aircraft needs monitoring, and several groups need the right information. I developed a proposed command-and-control architecture around those responsibilities.

I created the operating concept, functional breakdown, requirements structure, and interface matrix. Keeping the focus on the control center made the scope manageable while showing its connections to aircraft, ground stations, customers, and external services.
The result was a documented systems design for review and further requirements development. It was not an operating delivery service or a flight-test project.

story.heading: Choosing the control-center boundary
paragraphs: The project considered a command-and-control center for medical UAV delivery. A request from a healthcare facility has to become a feasible mission, while the aircraft, payload, ground services, and airspace coordination remain connected to the operation.

I developed the control-center operating concept, functional decomposition, requirements structure, and interface matrix. I placed the system boundary around the control center rather than claiming to design the aircraft or the entire logistics network.

The report identified practical dependencies: uneven communication coverage, telecommunications infrastructure outside the center’s control, fleet readiness, staffing, power, and airspace authorization. These constraints shape the architecture even before numerical performance targets are allocated.

sources.label: Stakeholders, constraints, and boundary, PDF pp. 7–9

story.heading: Turning an operation into assigned responsibilities
paragraphs: I organized the operation around five primary functions: plan missions, communicate, coordinate airspace, monitor, and manage the fleet. Their decomposition links an initial request to route feasibility, authorization, readiness checks, launch, supervision, intervention, and mission confirmation.

Separating the functions makes their responsibilities reviewable. For example, a route is not ready for launch merely because it is geometrically feasible: authorization and vehicle-readiness checks are also dependencies in the proposed requirements.
The functional flows describe planned behavior and information needs. They are not a deployed dispatch application, an autonomous flight controller, or evidence that a delivery was completed.

sources.label: Operating concept and functional flows, PDF pp. 9–15

story.heading: Examining the interfaces behind the diagrams
paragraphs: I used a product-level N² matrix to make coupling visible across the facility, power system, communications network, computing hardware, software, and operator consoles. Marking an interaction exposes an integration responsibility; it does not by itself define a data packet, failure response, or verified interface.

The requirements then distinguish internal and external interfaces and record their rationale. The examples below show the kinds of allocations needed before these relationships can become an implementable control system.

table.caption: Examples of proposed interface responsibilities
rows: Flight-plan submission and authorization before launch
Detailed interface agreement and response-time targets
Refresh rate, data age, and latency limits
A redundant path for command continuity
Battery, payload, link, and health checks

sources.label: Interface matrix and requirements, PDF pp. 17–22

story.heading: Writing requirements without pretending the numbers were finished
paragraphs: The requirements structure records functions, rationale, type, and interface category. It includes launch prerequisites, command and telemetry exchanges, redundant links, operator intervention, mission records, and fleet status.

Several performance values in the source remain X/XXX placeholders, including latency, refresh rate, failover timing, and uptime. One requirement also has an incomplete function reference. Those entries need resolution and traceability review before the document can be treated as an implementation baseline.

The illustrative mission timeline also overlaps planning and departure. It needs reconciliation with the stated prelaunch authorization and readiness requirements, rather than being presented as an approved operational sequence.

story.heading: The result and the next verification step
paragraphs: The result is a proposed architecture that connects the operating concept, functional responsibilities, product interfaces, and requirement categories. It gives a technical reviewer concrete boundaries and dependencies to examine.

There was no built UAV network, flight test, or measured service performance in this project. The next stage would allocate numerical targets, reconcile the timeline and traceability, and define verification methods for each requirement before implementation.

summary: A medical-drone mission depends on planning, communication, airspace approval, fleet readiness, and operator oversight. I developed the proposed control-center architecture that connects those responsibilities, including functional diagrams, an interface matrix, and requirements. The key decision was defining a clear system boundary while making external dependencies and unfinished performance targets explicit.

title: Functionally Graded Crash Boxes
tools: LS-DYNA, nonlinear impact modeling, comparative design analysis
imageAlt: Four simulated crash-box shapes during progressive collapse
takeaway: My thesis compared crash-box designs and showed how redistributing wall thickness changes their response to impact.
overviewHeading: Studying how a crash box absorbs impact.

report.title: Impact Analysis of Multi-Cell Crash Box Structures with Transverse Functionally Graded Thickness

figures.title: Progressive collapse in simulation
figures.caption: Four LS-DYNA states showing the modeled crash box folding during impact.
figures.alt: Four LS-DYNA simulation states showing a red crash box progressively crushing

figures.title: Uniform and graded wall thickness
figures.caption: The conventional multicell section (left) and a graded-thickness section (right). Both retain four cells while distributing wall material differently.
figures.alt: Side-by-side model cross sections showing a uniform four-cell tube and a four-cell tube with varying wall thickness.

description: Used impact simulations to study how internal walls and varying thickness change a crash box’s folding, energy absorption, and crushing force.
overview: A crash box absorbs energy by folding during an impact. In my undergraduate thesis, I studied how its internal walls and thickness distribution change that process.

I developed LS-DYNA models, checked the modeling approach against a published tube-crush experiment, and compared designs under the same simulated conditions. One graded design absorbed 124% more energy per unit of crushed material than a plain tube, and 11.8% more than a conventional multicell tube.

The same design had a 15.8% lower mean crushing force than the multicell comparison. These simulation results showed a tradeoff to consider in design selection; the proposed structures were not physically tested.

story.heading: Changing the section to control progressive collapse
paragraphs: A crash box absorbs impact energy through progressive folding. My undergraduate thesis investigated whether combining a four-cell section with thickness graded across its walls could change the folding response and energy absorption per unit of material being crushed.

I developed the LS-DYNA models and comparative studies. Plain square, conventional multicell, and graded-wall sections provided reference cases. A separate taper-ratio study varied the distribution of wall thickness rather than treating one geometry as universally best.

sources.label: Study geometry and loading, PDF pp. 48–56

story.heading: Keeping impact conditions consistent
paragraphs: The dynamic comparison used nominal 100 × 100 × 400 mm tubes, a fixed base, and a rigid 98 kg impactor moving axially at 13.4 m/s. This gives about 8.80 kJ of initial kinetic energy. Holding the loading conditions common made the section comparisons interpretable.

The model used solid elements with three elements through the wall thickness, following the convergence guidance in the cited literature. This should not be read as a new mesh-convergence study performed on every candidate. Contact definitions and energy controls were part of the numerical setup needed to follow large deformation and self-contact.
For the graded four-cell family, the taper ratio ranged from 1.5 to 2.75. At a ratio of 2, the geometry table specifies minimum and maximum wall thicknesses of 1 and 2 mm.

story.heading: Checking the numerical approach against published evidence
paragraphs: Before comparing the proposed impact structures, I reproduced a published aluminum-tube crush configuration and compared its response with the experimental benchmark. That physical experiment was performed by the cited researchers, not by me.

The benchmark comparison covered the force-displacement history and energy/force metrics. The peak-force agreement was weaker than the agreement in the integrated response. Matching one benchmark supports the modeling approach within that comparison; it does not physically validate every new geometry or a complete vehicle crash system.

story.heading: Defining the energy metric before comparing it
paragraphs: I evaluated absorbed energy, mean crushing force, specific energy absorption, and crushing-force efficiency alongside the folding sequence. The report defines specific energy absorption using displaced or crushed mass, rather than the total mass of the whole component.

For the taper-ratio-2 graded multicell case, the source reports 8.599 kJ absorbed, approximately 0.257 kg of crushed mass, and approximately 0.946 kg of total specimen mass. The reported SEA of 33.487 kJ/kg therefore uses the smaller, crushed-mass denominator. It must not be compared directly with values normalized by whole-component mass.

equation.spoken: Specific energy absorption equals absorbed energy divided by the mass of the crushed portion.
equation.explanation: This is the normalization used in the thesis. It is distinct from energy per total component mass.

sources.label: Energy definition and reported metrics, PDF pp. 82–84

story.heading: What improved, and what moved the other way
paragraphs: At taper ratio 2, the graded multicell model’s SEA was about 124% above the plain tube and 11.8% above the conventional multicell tube under the simulated conditions. Its mean crushing force was 15.8% lower than the conventional multicell result.

The taper study also showed SEA increasing from 30.742 to 36.129 kJ/kg as taper ratio increased from 1.5 to 2.75. These are numerical results for the selected geometry, material inputs, boundary conditions, and crushed-mass definition.

The useful design conclusion is the tradeoff, not a blanket claim that one section improves every crashworthiness measure. Energy absorption, force levels, mass basis, and available crush distance need to be considered together.

table.caption: Simulated SEA comparison at taper ratio 2 where applicable

story.heading: Limits of a simulation-led result
paragraphs: The proposed crash boxes were not physically manufactured or impact-tested in this study. Further work would need specimen tests, material and contact characterization, and additional numerical sensitivity checks before relying on the concepts in a vehicle design.

The source’s absolute force labels are inconsistent with its energy and displacement scales. I have therefore retained the documented relative comparison and energy-per-crushed-mass values, and have not presented the ambiguous absolute force units as verified results.

summary: In my undergraduate thesis, I used impact simulations to investigate how internal walls and graded thickness affect a crash box’s folding. A graded four-cell design improved energy absorption per crushed mass by 124% against a plain tube, while its mean crushing force was lower than the conventional multicell comparison.
